29 June 2001 (as BHP Billiton) | hq_location = [[Melbourne]], Victoria, Australia | website = {{URL|https://www.bhp.com}} }} [[File:BHP Billiton.png|thumb|The former BHP Billiton logo]] '''BHP Group Limited''', founded as the '''Broken Hill Proprietary Company''', is an Australian [[Multinational corporation|multinational]] mining and metals corporation. BHP was established in August 1885 in [[Broken Hill]] and is headquartered in [[Melbourne]], Victoria.{{cite news |title=Silverton |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/6088837 |access-date=21 August 2020 |work=[[The Argus (Melbourne)|The Argus]] |date=30 July 1885 |location=Melbourne, Vic. |page=10}} The company specialises in mining and selling [[iron ore]], [[copper]] and [[coal]]. '''BHP Billiton''' was formed in June 2001 through the merger of the Australian '''Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited''' (BHP) and the Anglo–Dutch '''Billiton plc''', trading on both the [[Australian Securities Exchange]] and [[London Stock Exchange]] as a [[dual-listed company]]. In 2015, some BHP Billiton assets were demerged and rebranded as [[South32]], while a scaled-down BHP Billiton became BHP. In 2018, BHP Billiton Limited and BHP Billiton plc became BHP Group Limited and BHP Group plc, respectively. In January 2022, BHP relinquished its London Stock Exchange listing, becoming a solely Australian Securities Exchange-listed company. As of 2025, BHP is the second largest public company in Australia,{{Cite web |title=Top 50 by Market Cap |url=https://www.asx.com.au/markets/trade-our-cash-market/equity-market-prices/top-50-market-cap |access-date=2025-12-10 |website=Australian Securities Exchange |language=en}} and the largest mining company in the world, both as measured by [[Market capitalization|market capitalisation]].{{Cite web |title=Largest mining companies by market cap 2021 |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/272706/top-10-mining-companies-worldwide-based-on-market-value/ |access-date=2022-03-08 |website=Statista }} In 2025, the company's position in the [[Forbes Global 2000|''Forbes'' Global 2000]] was 125th.{{Cite web |last=SCHIFRIN" |first="ANDREA MURPHY"," MATT |title=Forbes' 2025 Global 2000 List - The World’s Largest Companies Ranked |url=https://www.forbes.com/lists/global2000/ |access-date=2025-12-10 |website=Forbes |language=en}} ==History== ===Billiton=== [[File:Billiton logo.png|right|thumb|The former Billiton logo]] {{ill |Billiton Maatschappij |nl }} was founded 29 September 1860, when its articles of association were approved by a meeting of [[shareholder]]s in the {{lang |nl |Groot Keizershof}} hotel in [[The Hague]], Netherlands.{{cite book |last=van den Berg |first=Jurrien |editor1-last=Houben |editor1-first=V. (1999) ''A Future More Prosperous: The History of Newcastle Steelworks 1912–1999'', The Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited, Newcastle. p. 30. The first consignment of Broken Hill ore (48 [[Long ton|tons]], 5 [[Hundredweight|cwt]], 3 [[Grain (unit)|gr]]) was smelted at the Intercolonial Smelting and Refining Company's works at [[Spotswood, Victoria]], a suburb of Melbourne. Historian Christopher Jay notes: {{blockquote |text=The resulting 35,605 [[ounce]]s [{{convert|35,605|ozt|g|disp=out|abbr=off|link=on}}] of silver raised a lot of interest when exhibited at the City of Melbourne Bank in [[Collins Street, Melbourne|Collins Street]]. Some sceptics asserted the promoters were merely using silver from somewhere else, to ramp up the shares.... Another shareholder, the dominating [[W. R. Wilson]] had had to lend [[William Jamieson (mining)|William Jamieson]], General Manager, a new suit so he could take the first prospectus, printed at Silverton near Broken Hill on 20 June 1885, to Adelaide to start the float process.}} The geographic Broken Hill, for which the town was named, was discovered and named by Captain [[Charles Sturt]], stirring great interest among prospectors. Nothing of note was discovered until 5 November 1883, when [[Charles Rasp]], [[boundary rider]] for the surrounding [[Mount Gipps Station]], pegged out a {{convert|40|acre|ha|order=flip|adj=on}} claim with contractors David James and James Poole.Coulls, A. [https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/rasp-charles-4452 "Rasp, Charles (1846 - 1907)"], ''Australian Dictionary of Biography'', Volume 6. Melbourne University Press, 1976. p. 9. Together with a [[Syndicate of Seven|half-dozen backers]], including station manager [[George McCulloch (mine owner)|George McCulloch]] (a young cousin of Victorian Premier [[James McCulloch|Sir James McCulloch]]),Oxford Dictionary of National Biography Rasp formed the '''Broken Hill Company''' staking out the entire Hill. As costs mounted during the ensuing months of fruitless search, three of the original seven (now remembered as the [[Syndicate of Seven]]) sold their shares, so that, on the eve of the company's great success, there were nine shareholders, including Rasp, McCulloch, Philip Charly (aka Charley), David James, James Poole (five of the original syndicate of seven, which had previously included George Urquhart and G.A.M. Lind), Bowes Kelly, W. R. Wilson, and William Jamieson (who had bought shares from several of the founders).{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article11102036 |title=Treasure Hill on Sheep Station |newspaper=[[The Argus (Melbourne)|The Argus]] |location=Melbourne |date=2 September 1937 |access-date=20 July 2013 |page=8 |via=National Library of Australia}}{{cite book |title=United States Congressional Serial Set, Volume 2591 |date=1889 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |page=344 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VkZHAQAAIAAJ}} [[John Darling, Jr.]] became a director of the company in 1892 and was chairman of directors from 1907 to 1914.{{Australian Dictionary of Biography |first=H. S. K. |last=Kent |title=Darling, John (1852–1914) |id2=darling-john-3876 |access-date=5 December 2013}} Strongly encouraged by the [[New South Wales]] Minister for Public Works, [[Arthur Hill Griffith]],{{cite encyclopedia |title=Arthur Hill Griffith (1861–1946) |encyclopedia=[[Australian Dictionary of Biography]] |publisher=National Centre of Biography, Australian National University |url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/griffith-arthur-hill-6486 |access-date=26 July 2018 |last=Nairn |first=Bede |chapter= }}{{cite web |last=Cameron |first=David |title=On an island in the River: The establishment of the Walsh Island Dockyard & Engineering Works, Newcastle, 1910–1919 |url=http://www.reocities.com/Athens/acropolis/9968/aha97b.html |website=[[Reocities]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131123073533/http://www.reocities.com/Athens/acropolis/9968/aha97b.html |archive-date=23 November 2013 |date=1997}} in 1915, the company ventured into steel manufacturing, with its operations based primarily at the [[Newcastle Steelworks]]. The decision to move from mining ore at Broken Hill to opening a steelworks at Newcastle was due to the technical limitations in recovering value from mining the lower-lying sulphide ores.Jay, Christopher. (1999) ''A Future More Prosperous: The History of Newcastle Steelworks 1912–1999'', The Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited, Newcastle. p. 34. The discovery of [[Iron Knob]] and Iron Monarch near the western shore of the [[Spencer Gulf]] in [[South Australia]], combined with the refinement, by BHP metallurgists [[A. D. Carmichael]] and [[Leslie Bradford]], of the [[froth flotation]] technique for separating zinc sulphides from the accompanying [[gangue]] and subsequent conversion (Carmichael–Bradford process) to oxides of the metal, allowed BHP to economically extract valuable metals from the heaps of [[tailings]] up to {{convert|40|ft|order=flip}} high at the mine site.Jay, Christopher. (1999) ''A Future More Prosperous: The History of Newcastle Steelworks 1912–1999'', The Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited, Newcastle. pp. 42–43. In 1942, the [[Imperial Japanese Navy]] targeted the BHP steelworks{{cite news |url=https://www.newcastlemirage.com/stories/throwback-thursday-the-shelling-of-newcastle-by-amy-theodore|title=Throwback Thursday; The Shelling of Newcastle|first=Amy |last=Theodore|work=Newcastle Mirage|date=1 February 2018 |access-date=14 February 2018}} during the largely unsuccessful [[shelling of Newcastle]].{{cite book|last=Carruthers|first=Steven L.|title=Japanese Submarine Raiders, 1942 : A Maritime Mystery|year=2006|publisher=Casper Publications|location=Narrabeen, NSW|isbn=978-0-9775063-0-9|edition=Revised}} Newcastle operations were closed in 1999,{{cite news |url=http://www.abc.net.au/7.30/stories/s55787.htm |title=Steel City without the Big Australian |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000308060425/http://www.abc.net.au/7.30/stories/s55787.htm |work= [[7.30]]|date=29 September 1999 |archive-date=8 March 2000}} and a {{convert|70|ST|order=flip|adj=on}} commemorative sculpture, ''[[The Muster Point]]'', was installed on Industrial Drive, in the suburb of [[Mayfield, New South Wales]]. Tedi environmental disaster}} The '''Ok Tedi environmental disaster''' caused severe harm to the environment along the [[Ok Tedi River]] and the [[Fly River]] in the [[Western Province (Papua New Guinea)|Western Province]] of [[Papua New Guinea]] between around 1984 and 2013. In 1999, BHP reported that 90 million tons of mine waste was annually discharged into the river for more than ten years and destroyed downstream villages, agriculture and fisheries. Mine wastes were deposited along {{cvt|1000|km}} of the Ok Tedi and the Fly River below its confluence with the Ok Tedi, and over an area of {{cvt|100|km2}}. BHP's CEO, Paul Anderson, said that the Ok Tedi Mine was "not compatible with our environmental values and the company should never have become involved."{{cite news|last=Burton|first=Bob|date=13 August 1999|title=BHP admits Ok Tedi mine is environmental disaster|publisher=[[Asia Times|Asia Times Online]]|url=http://www.atimes.com/oceania/AH13Ah01.html|url-status=unfit|access-date=18 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000925131337/http://atimes.com/oceania/AH13Ah01.html|archive-date=25 September 2000}} In the 1990s the communities of the lower [[Western Province, Papua New Guinea|Fly Region]], including the [[Yonggom]] people,{{cite book|last=Kirsch|first=Stuart|url=http://www.sup.org/book.cgi?book_id=5342|title=Reverse Anthropology: Indigenous Analysis of Social and Environmental Relations in New Guinea|date=July 2006|publisher=[[Stanford University Press]]|isbn=0-8047-5342-3|pages=272|access-date=2007-05-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611202058/http://www.sup.org/book.cgi?book_id=5342|archive-date=2011-06-11|url-status=dead}} sued BHP and received US$28.6 million in an out-of-court settlement. Experts predict that it will take 300 years to clean up the toxic contamination.{{cite news|date=20 January 2007|title=Villagers sue BHP Billiton for $5bn|work=[[The Age]]|url=https://www.theage.com.au/news/business/villagers-sue-bhp-billiton-for-5bn/2007/01/19/1169095978975.html|access-date=4 February 2007}} === Bento Rodrigues dam collapse === {{Main|Mariana dam disaster}} [[File:Bento Rodrigues, Mariana, Minas Gerais (22828956680).jpg|thumb|A village flooded in the [[Bento Rodrigues dam disaster]] (2015). Later in July, the same court ordered BHP to begin the application process for [[Cerro Colorado mine|Cerro Colorado]] operating permits from scratch.{{Cite web |date=2022-01-05 |title=BHP's Cerro Colorado copper mine in Chile hit by further water measures |url=https://www.mining.com/bhps-cerro-colorado-mine-in-chile-hit-by-further-water-measures/ |access-date=2022-05-25 |website=mining.com |language=en-US}} In 2023 the mine was closed as its permit expired to extract water from the [[bofedal]]-hosting [[Pampa Lagunillas Aquifer|aquifer of Lagunillas]] expired and was not renewed. BHP subsidiary Pampa Norte plans to start works in 2028, with the intention of reopening Cerro Colorado around 2030.{{Cite news |title=BHP pone fecha a reapertura de Cerro Colorado: "usará agua de mar" y extenderá su vida por 20 años |last=Cárdenas |first=Leonardo |date=2024-08-08 |url=https://www.latercera.com/pulso-pm/noticia/bhp-pone-fecha-a-reapertura-de-cerro-colorado-usara-agua-de-mar-y-extendera-su-vida-por-20-anos/XYIYMRZQNNASRL2EUIUDFVMMT4/ |access-date=2025-05-26 |work=[[La Tercera]] |language=es}} Starting in 2022 indigenous [[Atacama people|Atacameño people]] sued BHP's [[Minera Escondida]], [[Albemarle Corporation|Albemarle]] and [[Zaldívar mine|Minera Zaldívar]] over damages to the [[Monturaqui-Negrillar-Tilopozo Aquifer]]. The lawsuit was joined by the Chilean state's Consejo de Defensa del Estado. BHP Group Limited, founded as the Broken Hill Proprietary Company, is an Australian multinational mining and metals corporation. BHP was established in August 1885 in Broken Hill and is headquartered in Melbourne, Victoria. The company specialises in mining and selling iron ore, copper and coal.
BHP Billiton was formed in June 2001 through the merger of the Australian Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited (BHP) and the Anglo–Dutch Billiton plc, trading on both the Australian Securities Exchange and London Stock Exchange as a dual-listed company.
In 2015, some BHP Billiton assets were demerged and rebranded as South32, while a scaled-down BHP Billiton became BHP. In 2018, BHP Billiton Limited and BHP Billiton plc became BHP Group Limited and BHP Group plc, respectively. In January 2022, BHP relinquished its London Stock Exchange listing, becoming a solely Australian Securities Exchange-listed company. 
As of 2025, BHP is the second largest public company in Australia, and the largest mining company in the world, both as measured by market capitalisation. In 2025, the company's position in the Forbes Global 2000 was 125th.
